stages.stage_name: Open Input Data and Measurement Evidence
stages.score_derivation: The evidence shows moderate but incomplete input-data traceability. The README identifies that GFW map layers and relevant datasets are stored in the Resource Watch API and provides a query endpoint for GFW datasets; the API documentation describes dataset, layer, vocabulary, metadata, legend, and interaction fields; and calculation docs identify some underlying columns and a Geotrellis table UUID used for biomass/carbon widgets. This is enough to show that some inputs are externally identifiable and structured. The score is not lower because there are concrete public pointers to data infrastructure and metadata conventions. It is not higher because the bundle does not include the actual datasets, primary measurement sources, dataset licenses, version identifiers, update histories, quantified uncertainties, quality-control documentation, or traceability from secondary API datasets back to primary satellite/measurement evidence.
stages.uncertainty: Medium uncertainty: the public API may contain richer metadata, but the supplied bundle only documents access patterns and schemas, not the full input evidence chain.

references.label: README identifies dataset source API
references.quote_or_finding: “GFW Map layers and relevant datasets are stored in the RW-API” and an endpoint is provided: https://api.resourcewatch.org/v1/dataset?app=gfw&includes=layer,vocabulary,metadata&page[size]=200.
references.relevance: Shows that input datasets and layers are at least identifiable through an external API, supporting a moderate score.

references.label: GFW API dataset and metadata schema
references.quote_or_finding: Documents dataset syntax, vocabulary tags, metadata keys, layer syntax, ISO country fields, and legend/application configuration for GFW layers.
references.relevance: Supports traceability of how datasets are represented in the application, but it is schema documentation rather than the underlying measurement evidence.

references.label: Climate widget input column and table reference
references.quote_or_finding: Above-ground biomass is said to come from the `whrc_aboveground_biomass_stock_2000__Mg` column within summary Geotrellis tables, with an example table UUID `998dd97a-389f-4a02-988f-17b184f507ac`.
references.relevance: Provides a concrete example of a derived environmental input being linked to a named column and table identifier.

stages.score_derivation: There is strong evidence that the GFW web application software is open source: the GitHub repository is public, has an MIT license, includes setup instructions, identifies the main framework stack, and contains documentation for widget calculations and layer/dataset configuration. The score is not lower because the software license, repository metadata, installation commands, and method documentation are explicit. It is not higher because the evidence mainly covers the front-end web app; the bundle does not include complete evidence for all upstream analytical services, APIs, data pipelines, model code, dependency lockfiles, infrastructure-as-code, or independent operation of the full system without Heroku, Resource Watch API, and other external services.
stages.uncertainty: Low-to-medium uncertainty: the repository evidence is clear for the web app, but the supplied bundle does not establish openness of every model, backend, and data-processing component used by GFW claims.

references.label: Repository metadata and license
references.quote_or_finding: Repository description: “Global Forest Watch: An online, global, near-real time forest monitoring tool”; license listed as MIT; default branch is `develop`.
references.relevance: Shows a public version-controlled software repository with a recognized open-source license.

references.label: MIT license text
references.quote_or_finding: The license permits use, copy, modification, merge, publication, distribution, sublicensing, and sale of the software under MIT terms.
references.relevance: Supports openness and reusability of the software code.

references.label: README setup and stack
references.quote_or_finding: The app is built with Next.js, React, and Redux; setup commands include `git clone`, `yarn`, copying `.env.sample` to `.env.local`, and `yarn dev`.
references.relevance: Provides practical method/software documentation for understanding and running the web app.

references.label: Widget calculation methods
references.quote_or_finding: Documents statistical calculations for widgets, including weekly aggregation, zero filling, means, standard deviations, and smoothing.
references.relevance: Shows that at least some analytical methods behind displayed indicators are inspectable in documentation.

stages.score_derivation: The project has partial execution and reproducibility evidence. The README gives commands to run the web app locally and describes deployment from `develop` and `master`; CI workflows define linting and unit tests on fixed Node version 18.15.0; and CodeQL analysis is configured. These are meaningful execution artifacts for software reproducibility. The score is not lower because an external actor can plausibly install, run, lint, and test the front-end. It is not higher because the evidence does not provide exact workflow runs connecting specific environmental inputs to specific reported outputs, does not include captured outputs, parameters, API snapshots, dataset versions, production environment variables, or a reproducible computational environment for the full data-to-claim pipeline. Running the web app is not the same as reproducing the underlying forest-monitoring results.
stages.uncertainty: Medium uncertainty: more reproducibility information may exist in files not included in the bundle, but the supplied evidence lacks full run-level provenance.

references.relevance: Shows an inspectable high-level execution/deployment process, though not full scientific run provenance.

stages.score_derivation: The evidence shows some linkage across components, but it is not sufficiently explicit or versioned to trace specific environmental claims end-to-end. The README links the web app to Resource Watch API datasets and to layer-manager; API documentation explains how dataset metadata keys and layer configurations drive what appears in the app; and the climate widget documentation links a calculation to a specific column and example Geotrellis table UUID. These are concrete positive signs, so the score is not lower. single_paragraph_summary: The supplied evidence supports a moderate Open Traceability score for the GFW web app. The strongest dimension is open-source software: the public GitHub repository, MIT license, setup instructions, CI, and calculation documentation make the front-end application and some methods inspectable. Publications and communication are also reasonably supported through the public dashboard description and method documents. However, input-data traceability, execution reproducibility, community review, and especially end-to-end linkage remain incomplete in the bundle: the evidence points to the Resource Watch API and some dataset/schema conventions, but does not provide primary measurement provenance, dataset versions, quantified uncertainties, exact workflow runs, archived outputs, or claim-level links among data, code, computations, review records, and public claims.
limitations: The assessment uses only the supplied evidence bundle and does not inspect the live Resource Watch API, live Global Forest Watch website, GitHub issues, pull requests, releases, or repository files not included in the bundle.

The project URL is for the GFW web app, not necessarily the full Global Forest Watch scientific data-processing system; upstream APIs, satellite data pipelines, alert-generation models, and backend services may have separate repositories or documentation not included here.
No actual API responses, dataset records, primary measurement documentation, dataset licenses, uncertainty estimates, or quality-control reports were supplied.
No specific environmental claim or dashboard output was supplied, so linkage was assessed from general repository documentation rather than from a claim-specific evidence chain.
The evidence bundle includes workflow configuration but not CI run logs, exact production environment configuration, API snapshots, or reproducible computational runs for environmental results.
The evidence bundle reports open issue counts and workflows but does not include actual review discussions, governance records, peer-review materials, or correction histories.

single_paragraph_summary: Global Forest Watch’s public web-app repository provides strong open-source evidence for the software layer: the code is public, MIT-licensed, documented for local development, and supported by CI, CodeQL, release practices, and method documents for some widgets. The project also exposes partial data and method traceability through Resource Watch API references, dataset/layer metadata schemas, and calculation documentation linking some formulas to named inputs. However, the supplied evidence does not establish a fully inspectable environmental evidence chain from specific public claims to primary datasets, dataset versions, uncertainties, code commits, configurations, execution runs, review records, and publication artifacts. As a result, the project scores well on open software and reasonably on communication, but only moderately or weakly on input-data provenance, reproducible execution, community/scientific review, and explicit cross-stage linkage.
limitations: The assessment uses only the supplied evidence bundle and did not inspect the live Global Forest Watch site, API responses, GitHub issues, pull requests, releases, or files not included in the bundle.

single_paragraph_summary: The supplied evidence shows that the GFW web app is substantially open as software: it is in a public GitHub repository, MIT licensed, documented for local development, and supported by CI, CodeQL, deployment, API, and widget-calculation documentation. It also provides partial traceability from the app to Resource Watch API datasets/layers and, for some widgets, to formulas and example table/column identifiers. However, the evidence chain is much weaker for primary environmental input data, measurement provenance, uncertainty, dataset licensing/versioning, complete backend/data-processing workflows, exact reproducible runs, and explicit claim-level links from public dashboard values to dataset versions, code commits, model configurations, reviews, and publications. Overall, this is a moderately traceable open-source environmental web platform, with strong front-end software openness but incomplete end-to-end open traceability for environmental claims.

No primary satellite or field measurement datasets were provided, so provenance, quality control, uncertainty, and reuse conditions for input data could not be fully assessed.

The live Global Forest Watch website and Resource Watch API may contain additional documentation or metadata, but only the supplied artifacts were used for scoring.

stages.score_derivation: The project has a public homepage, a public GitHub README explaining that GFW is a dynamic online forest monitoring and alert system, and documentation for API layer/dataset configuration and widget calculations. These materials support public communication and some scrutiny of displayed indicators and methods. The score is not lower because the documents include concrete formulas and schema explanations rather than only marketing descriptions. The score is not higher because the evidence bundle does not include specific reports, papers, dashboard pages, indicator version histories, update-cycle documentation, data-source citations in final outputs, review status of publications, or open content licensing for the website/publications. For a dynamic dashboard, the supplied evidence is insufficient to verify that all claims are clearly tied to sources, update cycles, and versions.
stages.uncertainty: Medium: the public website may contain more communication and source documentation, but the bundle only includes repository documentation and metadata.

stages.score_derivation: There is some linkage across the evidence chain: the README links the web app to the Resource Watch API endpoint for GFW datasets, API documentation explains how metadata keys and layer configurations connect API records to application behavior, and calculation docs connect certain widget outputs to formulas and, in one case, to a named source column and table identifier. This prevents a very low score. However, the chain is not explicit, specific, versioned, or externally verifiable end-to-end. The supplied evidence does not link particular environmental claims or dashboard values to exact dataset versions, primary measurement records, code commits, model configurations, workflow runs, CI artifacts, review discussions, publication versions, or archived outputs. single_paragraph_summary: The wri/gfw repository provides strong open-source evidence for the Global Forest Watch web application itself: it is public, MIT-licensed, documented for local setup, and includes calculation notes, API/layer schema documentation, CI, CodeQL, and release/deployment practices. Traceability is much weaker for the underlying environmental evidence chain: the bundle points to external Resource Watch API datasets and gives some formula-to-column links, but it does not include primary measurement provenance, dataset licenses, uncertainty/quality-control documentation, versioned data snapshots, exact production workflow runs, or explicit claim-to-data-to-code-to-review linkages. Overall, this is a substantially open web-app and methods repository with only partial end-to-end open traceability for the environmental claims displayed by the system.
limitations: The evidence bundle contains selected repository files but not the full repository tree, package manifests, lockfiles, tests, source-code implementations, or environment templates.
The Resource Watch API endpoint is referenced, but the bundle does not include API responses, dataset metadata records, data licenses, data versions, or primary measurement provenance.

No live Global Forest Watch dashboard pages, reports, publications, or indicator pages were included, so publication quality and source citation in final outputs could only be inferred from repository documentation.
No actual GitHub issues, pull requests, review comments, release pages, correction notices, or community discussions were supplied, only metadata and workflow descriptions.
No archived workflow runs, production run logs, model configuration files, data-processing pipelines, containers, or reproducibility packages were provided.
Scores assess the supplied evidence only and may understate traceability if relevant artifacts exist outside the bundle.
